issues.legal_issue: A dispute over whether property claimed as waqf property is waqf property must be determined by the Waqf Tribunal when that question falls within the Tribunal’s statutory jurisdiction.
material_facts: The Board sued for an injunction concerning land it claimed was waqf property.
The respondent denied that the land was waqf property and challenged the Board’s title.
The suit was transferred to the Tribunal, which rejected the respondent’s challenge to its jurisdiction.
issues.conclusion: The Tribunal had jurisdiction to decide whether the land was waqf property, and the civil court’s jurisdiction was barred for that issue; the High Court erred in holding otherwise.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 6(1), 7(1), 83 and 85 of the Wakf Act, 1995, a question whether listed property is waqf property is for the Tribunal, and the civil-court bar applies to matters the Act requires the Tribunal to decide. The explanation to Section 6(1) includes a person interested in the property even if not interested in the waqf, subject to the notice requirement. The Court applied Haryana Wakf Board v. Mahesh Kumar and distinguished the earlier interpretation in Board of Muslim Wakfs, Rajasthan v. Radha Kishan in light of the later statutory explanation.

predicates.civil_suit_concerning_claimed_waqf_prope: A civil suit concerns property that one side claims is waqf property.
predicates.defendant_denies_waqf_status: The opposing party asserts that the property is not waqf property.
predicates.status_question_within_tribunal_authorit: The governing waqf framework assigns the disputed question of the property’s waqf status to the Tribunal.

issues.definition: When a civil suit concerns property claimed as waqf property, the opposing party denies that status, and the Tribunal is assigned the status question, the Tribunal has jurisdiction to decide it.

issues.legal_issue: A suit seeking possession from a lessee of waqf property is not within the Tribunal’s jurisdiction under the pre-amendment statutory scheme where that scheme did not assign eviction disputes to it.
material_facts: The Board sought possession and an injunction against a person who had occupied the property as its lessee.
The Board claimed that the lease had ended and that the occupant had not returned possession.
The suit was filed before the statutory amendment expressly adding eviction and lessor-lessee disputes to the Tribunal’s jurisdiction.
issues.conclusion: The possession suit was triable by the civil court, and the High Court correctly directed that the plaint be returned for presentation there.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 83 and 85 of the Wakf Act, 1995, as they stood before the 2013 amendment, civil-court jurisdiction was excluded only for matters required by the Act to be determined by the Tribunal. The Act then provided no Tribunal proceeding for eviction of a tenant or determination of the lessor’s and lessee’s rights and obligations. The Court applied Ramesh Gobindram v. Sugra Humayun Mirza Wakf and Faseela M. v. Munnerul Islam Madrasa Committee; it also noted that the 2013 amendment expressly added eviction and lessor-lessee disputes, but did not govern these suits.

predicates.waqf_suit_seeking_possession_from_lessee: A suit concerning waqf property seeks possession from a person who occupied it as a lessee.
predicates.claim_is_eviction_or_lessor_lessee_dispu: The claim depends on ending the lease or resolving rights and obligations between lessor and lessee.
predicates.tribunal_law_at_filing_did_not_assign_ev: When the suit was filed, the applicable Tribunal jurisdiction did not include eviction or lessor-lessee disputes.

issues.definition: If a waqf suit seeks possession from a lessee over an eviction or lease dispute and the applicable Tribunal jurisdiction does not include those disputes, the civil court has jurisdiction over the possession claim.

issues.legal_issue: The one-year period for challenging a published list of waqfs applies to a person challenging the listed status of property if that person received a reasonable opportunity to represent their case during the relevant inquiry.
material_facts: The Court considered who is subject to the one-year period for bringing a suit disputing whether property included in a published waqf list is waqf property.

The statutory explanation includes a person interested in the property even if that person is not interested in the waqf, where a reasonable opportunity to present the person’s case was provided by notice during the inquiry.
issues.conclusion: The one-year period applies to persons challenging the list who received the required notice and opportunity; the list’s finality does not bind a person who was not given that opportunity.
issues.legal_principle: Section 6(1) and its proviso and explanation, read with Section 4’s inquiry and notice requirement, make the one-year period applicable to persons challenging the list, except those not served notice during the inquiry. The Court applied the interpretation of the materially similar explanation in Punjab Wakf Board v. Gram Panchayat and explained how the later statutory explanation affects the earlier ruling in Board of Muslim Wakfs, Rajasthan v. Radha Kishan.

predicates.suit_challenges_published_waqf_list: A person brings a suit disputing whether property included in a published waqf list is waqf property.
predicates.reasonable_inquiry_notice_given: The person received notice and a reasonable opportunity to present their case during the inquiry concerning the property.

issues.definition: When a suit challenges a published waqf list and the challenger received notice and a reasonable opportunity to be heard during the inquiry, the one-year limitation applies to that challenge.
